newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar drops briefly below 118 yen, then rebounds.
newsitem.headline: Dollar drops briefly below 118 yen, then rebounds.

text.p: The dollar dropped briefly below 118 yen in early Tokyo trade on Monday -- its lowest level in nearly four months -- but then rebounded to lick its wounds after the early panic selling.

Traders said the sharp decline reflected concern that the U.S. currency has turned the corner after a two-year rebound -- fears fanned by speculation that the interest-rate gap between the United States and Japan will narrow.

But some Asian dealers said economic fundamentals were being ignored in a scramble to unload U.S. dollar positions. "At this level, nobody is interested in buying," a commercial bank dealer in Tokyo said.
On Friday, the dollar plunged against the yen from an Asian session high of 123.72 yen to a U.S. session low of about 119.10 yen, the largest intra-day fall since September 1995.
The greenback fell as low as 117.60 yen on Monday morning here before rebounding to around 119 yen.
The dollar's latest drop followed comments by Japanese finance officials over the weekend expressing satisfaction over the yen's recent gains.

Asked over the weekend if a nearly six-yen rise against the dollar over the previous week was excessive, Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" for his influence over currency markets, said: "No, it is not overly excessive."

Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, in the southern Japanese city of Fukuoka along with Sakakibara for a meeting of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), said he believed the yen's rise indicated that foreign exchange markets were finally digesting a Group of Seven (G7) statement made last month on currency stability.

Financial leaders of the G7 -- Japan, the United States, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- said in Washington last month that they would monitor exchange rates and cooperate as appropriate. They said currency values should reflect fundamentals and excess volatility was not desirable.

A weak yen has been a clear plus for Japan's economy because of the boost it gives to exports by making them more price competitive, but the Japanese currency's slide had also raised concern about a resurgence of Tokyo's trade surplus and future trade friction with Washington.

Currency market players now appear to have sold dollars and bought yen on the belief that Tokyo's growing trade surplus will put upward pressure on the Japanese currency, while a possible shrinking of the interest rate gap between the United States and Japan will make the greenback less attractive.

Dealers said the market would focus for now on moves in Japanese market interest rates. If those rates rise further, expectations of a narrower U.S.-Japan interest-rate gap will keep the yen well-bid.
Japan has kept its interest rates at rockbottom levels since September 1995, when it slashed its official discount rate to 0.5 percent to keep its economic recovery on track.

Speculation has emerged that the Bank of Japan may be considering tightening its hyper-easy credit stance due to growing confidence in the recovery. But doubts remain whether the central bank will do so quickly, given persistent worries over the bad-loan burden at many Japanese financial institutions.
Comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan in New York on Friday, meanwhile, left room for doubt over whether the Fed would raise rates when it next meets on May 20.
